title: Algebra, exponents, and logarithms
note: Exponent rules come from counting factors: xᵃ · xᵇ has a + b factors of x. A logarithm asks for an exponent: logₐ x = y means aʸ = x, so log rules mirror exponent rules (products become sums, powers become multipliers).

items.ex: x² · x³ = x⁵: five factors of x in all.

items.c: logₐ x in terms of ln
items.ex: Change of base: log₂ 10 = ln 10 / ln 2 ≈ 3.32.

read.title: Logarithms undo exponentials
text: An exponential function like 2ˣ takes an exponent and returns a power: 2⁵ = 32. A logarithm runs the other direction. It takes the power and returns the exponent, so log₂ 32 = 5. Every log statement is an exponent statement in disguise: logₐ x = y says exactly the same thing as aʸ = x.

That is why the log rules look the way they do. When you multiply powers of the same base, you add exponents, so the log of a product is the sum of the logs: ln(xy) = ln x + ln y. Dividing subtracts exponents, so ln(x/y) = ln x − ln y. Raising a power to a power multiplies exponents, so ln(xʳ) = r ln x.

Calculus leans hardest on the natural logarithm, ln x, whose base is e ≈ 2.718. Because ln and eˣ are inverses, ln(eˣ) = x for every x and e^(ln x) = x whenever x > 0. These two facts let you solve equations: to free x from an exponent, take ln of both sides; to free x from a logarithm, exponentiate both sides. Remember that ln x only accepts positive inputs, because no power of e is zero or negative.

q.q: Which exponent fact explains ln(xy) = ln x + ln y?
o: Raising a power to a power multiplies exponents
Any nonzero number to the zero power is 1

q.q: How do you free x from an exponent, as in eˣ = 7?
Why must the input of ln x be positive?
o: No power of e is zero or negative
ln x is defined only for whole numbers
